title: The Song in the Missing Crate
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 41 of 50
content:
Greg's guitar came back smelling of rosemary.

That was our first clue something had gone wrong.

He'd lent it to the Lanternweald for a community concert and expected to collect it from Starwake Pier on Tuesday. Instead, on Wednesday morning, an envelope arrived from Moonroot Archive thanking him for the donation of an ‘instrument of uncertain educational purpose.’

He read the letter twice.

Then he put on the expression that meant he was trying very hard not to say a thing about people who needed music lessons.

“Educational purpose,” he repeated.

I leaned over the table. “You do look like a cautionary tale.”

“Fair. But they could at least call it a guitar.”

We went through the Starwake Door carrying the case the archive had returned. Greg opened it halfway down the pier and stopped.

Inside lay somebody else's instrument.

A small handmade flute rested in blue cloth. Beside it was a scrap of music, six measures written in ink so faint it almost disappeared in the sunlight.

Greg held the flute carefully. “Okay. That's not mine.”

“It has the same case.”

“Then somebody really wanted these things to look like they belonged together.”

He was no longer joking.

I recognized the kind of quiet that follows a loss too small to explain to a stranger. His guitar was not a famous artifact. It was worn, repaired, and comfortable in his hands. He'd written songs on it when he couldn't make himself say what the words were about.

I touched the edge of the case.

“We'll find it.”

He swallowed. “I know.”

“You don't sound convinced.”

“It's just a guitar.”

I looked at him.

He gave me a crooked smile. “Yeah. I heard it too.”

At Lanternwell Square we found Iroh serving tea and trying to keep two repair crews from standing beneath the same loose lantern. Toph sat on a wall arguing with Danse over a bent brass gear. Katara and Aang were hanging notices. Severus was inspecting a packet of medicinal herbs as though it had personally offended him.

For a moment I was struck by the strangeness of it all.

Not the magical doors. Not the impossible mixture of people from other places.

The ordinary fact that everyone had come because something needed doing.

Greg lifted the flute. “Anybody lose a piece of very serious music?”

Aang turned. “Actually, yes.”

He had been looking for the instrument to give to a student at his cultural school. It was a handmade practice flute, not ceremonial, but the student's grandfather had carved it and there was no way to replace the particular wear of the player's fingers.

Greg turned it over to him.

Aang's relief was immediate and entirely unguarded.

“Thank you.”

“Hey, no problem.”

I touched Greg's elbow. “Your guitar.”

Aang's expression fell.

“We'll help,” he said.

Greg shook his head. “Not your fault.”

“Maybe not,” I said, “but we're all here now.”

Neri brought us a list. There were fourteen misplaced parcels and three missing altogether. Greg's instrument was one of the missing ones. Another was a shipment of seed, and the third a bundle of handwritten letters intended for Jasmine Steps.

“We think somebody replaced the destination tags,” Neri explained.

“On purpose?” Greg asked.

“We don't know.”

He looked at the list.

“Maybe the problem isn't just where they went.”

“What do you mean?”

“Maybe somebody doesn't want to give them back.”

I watched Neri's expression change. It wasn't guilt exactly. More the dawning awareness that generosity and taking were not interchangeable.

We divided the search by places where the missing parcels might have been stored while the bell was misbehaving. I took the archive. Greg took the pier. We agreed to meet by the old notice board in an hour and promised not to wander off into any other universe without telling one another.

The archive smelled like rain caught between pages.

Severus showed me a storeroom. He did not comment on the fact that I had arrived searching for a guitar and seemed disappointed to find only books. Instead he handed me a notebook.

“Whoever has been moving things,” he said, “has attempted to classify them as ‘unclaimed.’”

“That's not a category.”

“It is when one wishes to make responsibility disappear.”

The word sat badly in my stomach.

I thought about the ways people disappear when no one writes their names down. The ways songs turn into stories and stories turn into things somebody claims to have invented.

I opened the notebook.

On the first page was a list of objects, each with a little box beside it. Guitars. Books. Medicine. A flute. Several crates of tea.

On the second page was a phrase underlined three times:

NO ONE NEEDS PERMISSION TO MAKE THINGS USEFUL.

It sounded kind.

It also sounded exactly like something a person could use to take whatever they wanted.

I found Greg in the square, sitting on the ground beside the repaired notice board. His guitar lay open across his knees. A new string had been fitted badly, but the old scratches were there. So was the little mark near the neck where he'd dropped it years ago and told me the story twice, each time changing how foolish he'd been.

He wasn't playing.

“Where was it?” I asked.

“Behind the storeroom, with a note about public use.”

“Did they hurt it?”

He plucked a string. It twanged.

“Only my dignity.”

I sat beside him.

“You okay?”

He shrugged. Then he stopped shrugging.

“I keep thinking I should be grateful they gave it back.”

“You can be glad it's back and angry someone took it.”

He looked at me for a long moment. “Yeah.”

We sat with that for a while. The square went on around us: hammering, conversation, the scrape of chairs, the warm sweet smell of bread. Eventually Greg tried the song on the scrap of music. The melody was hesitant but lovely, something that kept stepping toward a note and finding an unexpected turn instead.

“That's pretty,” I said.

“It's incomplete.”

“Most things worth keeping are.”

He played the phrase again and added a simple chord of his own. I leaned against his shoulder. He smelled like seawater, wood polish, and home.

“Does it bother you,” he asked, “that I make everything into a song?”

“Only when you use it to avoid saying what you mean.”

He stopped playing.

“And what do I mean now?”

“You were scared you wouldn't get something back.”

He nodded.

“Yeah.”

I took his hand. “I don't need you to make that sound cheerful.”

Greg put the guitar down. He kissed me softly, then laughed against my mouth because a hammer fell somewhere behind us and Toph shouted an opinion about workmanship.

“Romantic atmosphere,” he whispered.

“Unbeatable.”

We went back to the pier carrying the guitar between us. In the fading light, Greg played the little flute melody again. People slowed to listen. Some stayed. Some continued through their doors.

That was fine.

At the end, an older woman standing near the Lanternwell began to cry.

I went to her.

“Do you know that song?”

She nodded.

“My sister wrote it,” she said. “Before the last keeper closed the records room.”

Greg's fingers stilled.

I looked toward the square.

The melody was incomplete because somebody had taken its second page.

And for the first time that day, we had a person who might know why.
